title: The tenth week
subtitle: The baby is sleeping in longer stretches and you are starting to feel like a person again. Both are real.

baby.development: Your baby is reaching for toys, bringing them to the mouth, and holding their head steady. They may be starting to roll from front to back.

you.body: Your hair is shedding. Your joints are still loose. If you are exercising, the pelvic floor is the thing to watch, not the scale.
you.mind: The first three months are the hardest and they are almost over. If you are still feeling flat every day, that is worth a call rather than another month of waiting.

coreActions.title: Stop swaddling once the baby shows signs of rolling
coreActions.why: A swaddled baby who rolls onto their front cannot push back up, and that is the risk swaddling carries past the newborn stage.
coreActions.detail: Signs to watch for: rolling to one side, pushing up on the arms, or getting halfway over. When you see any of them, switch to a sleep sack with arms free. Some babies roll at three months, most by five.

coreActions.title: Learn the wake window for this age
coreActions.why: A baby who is put down at the right level of tired settles faster than one who is overtired or not tired yet.
coreActions.detail: At two to three months, most babies manage about 75 to 120 minutes awake between sleeps. Watch for the first yawn and the first eye rub, and start the wind-down then. A second wind means you waited too long.

coreActions.title: Check in on your mood, on purpose
coreActions.why: Postpartum depression can start at any point in the first year, not just the first six weeks.
coreActions.detail: The screening questions are about the last seven days. If you would answer them differently than you would have a month ago, say so at the next visit. The maternal mental health line is free and answers 24 hours a day.

alsoKnow.title: A flat spot is easier to fix now than later
alsoKnow.body: If the back of the head is flattening on one side, more tummy time and alternating the head position at sleep usually help. Ask the pediatrician at the four-month visit.

alsoKnow.title: Drool is not teething yet
alsoKnow.body: Most babies drool heavily from two months because the salivary glands are working before the swallowing is coordinated. First teeth usually arrive between four and seven months.

redFlags.text: A fever of 100.4°F or higher in a baby under three months
Fast or labored breathing, or a blue tint around the lips
Feeling hopeless most of the day, or thoughts of harming yourself or the baby

sources.title: A parent's guide to safe sleep
